heading: Two runners, one track
body:
**Floyd's Cycle Detection** uses two pointers: `slow` moves 1 step, `fast` moves 2 steps.

- If they **meet** → cycle exists
- If `fast` hits `None` → no cycle

Think of a track: a faster runner will lap a slower one if it loops.

heading: Why O(1) space wins
body:
The two-pointer trick uses **only 2 variables**, no matter how long the list.

Alternative: track visited nodes in a **set** → O(n) space.

Floyd's algorithm detects cycles **without extra memory**.

label: Crux · Python

q: Why does Floyd's cycle detection algorithm use O(1) space instead of O(n)?
options: It only uses two pointers regardless of list size, whereas the set-based approach stores every visited node
It modifies the linked list in-place to mark visited nodes
It uses recursion with tail-call optimization
It compresses the linked list data structure
explain: Two pointer variables = constant space. Set-based approach stores every visited node = O(n) space.
